The City of God
SIT-ee uhv GOD
theological work
From Latin De Civitate Dei; city (a commonwealth, a body of citizens) and God; Augustine’s great treatise contrasting the two cities.

📖 Biblical Definition

The City of God is the great work of Augustine of Hippo, begun after the sack of Rome in the early fifth century, when pagans charged that the abandonment of the old gods for Christ had brought the empire low. Augustine answered with a vast meditation on history, dividing all mankind into two cities distinguished by two loves: the earthly city, built by the love of self even to the contempt of God, and the heavenly city, built by the love of God even to the contempt of self. These two cities, intermingled in this present age, run through all history from the fall to the last judgment, when they shall be finally separated—the one to everlasting punishment, the other to eternal life. Augustine demolished the pretensions of pagan religion and philosophy, expounded the providence of God over the rise and fall of empires, and set the believer’s true citizenship in heaven, a pilgrim in the earthly city but a member of the city that has foundations. The dictionary honors Augustine as the greatest of the Latin fathers, whose doctrine of grace the Reformers gladly claimed, and whose two-cities framework remains a profound guide to the Christian’s posture in the world. Some elements of his ecclesiology were later pressed in directions the Reformation rejected, but the central vision—two cities, two loves, one final judgment—is biblical and enduring.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Augustine’s monumental treatise contrasting the earthly city, built on love of self, with the heavenly city, built on love of God—two cities running through all history to the last judgment.

expand to see more

THE CITY OF GOD, the great treatise of Augustine of Hippo.

Written after the sack of Rome to answer the charge that Christianity had ruined the empire.

Divides mankind into two cities marked by two loves—love of self and love of God.

Traces the two cities, intermingled now, through history to their final separation.

Sets the believer’s true citizenship in heaven, a pilgrim in the earthly city.

📖 Key Scripture

Heb 11:10 — "For he looked for a city which hath foundations, whose builder and maker is God."

Php 3:20 — "For our conversation is in heaven; from whence also we look for the Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ:"

Heb 13:14 — "For here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come."

Psa 46:4 — "There is a river, the streams whereof shall make glad the city of God, the holy place of the tabernacles of the most High."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Augustine’s two-cities vision is flattened into mere politics, or its doctrine of grace is severed from the medieval church that misapplied his ecclesiology.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the antithesis of the two cities: all history is the contest of two loves, the love of self that builds Babylon and the love of God that builds Jerusalem, intermingled until the judgment divides them forever. Against the modern reduction of Augustine to a political theorist or a culture-warrior on either side, the dictionary keeps his vision eschatological—the believer is a pilgrim whose citizenship is in heaven and who here has no continuing city.

A discerning reader honors Augustine’s doctrine of grace, which the Reformers claimed as their own against the Pelagians, while marking that his identification of the city of God with the visible church was later pressed by Rome into a defense of papal and ecclesiastical power the Reformation rightly rejected. The corruption is not in Augustine’s central vision but in its later misuse to exalt the institutional church. The two cities are not Rome and the barbarians, nor church and state simply, but the company of the redeemed and the company of the lost, known finally to God alone.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

The title sets the city of God against the earthly city, naming two commonwealths divided by their loves and destined for opposite ends.

expand to see more

Latin civitas — a city, a commonwealth, a body of citizens; the title word.

The original, De Civitate Dei contra Paganos, “on the city of God against the pagans.”

The biblical “city of God” — Zion, Jerusalem, and the heavenly city of Hebrews 11 and 12.

Augustine’s two cities are marked by amor sui, love of self, and amor Dei, love of God.

The framework draws on Babylon and Jerusalem as the two cities of Scripture.
